messages:
maria: Quick check-in on the queue <> scheduler refactor — I pushed the branch that extracts the queue topology (sharding, lane mapping) into a standalone component. Wanted to surface the tradeoffs we discussed and get 👀 on rollout plan.

alex: Saw the diff, looks cleaner. Biggest question: do we keep the admission policy logic inside scheduler or move to an admission controller service?

maria: My current draft moves admission into a thin controller that's invoked by the scheduler runtime. Pros: easier to test and hot-swap policies. Cons: extra RPC hop for very hot paths.

kevin: Extra hop is meh if it's local in-proc or unix-socket. We should measure p99 impact. Also worry about increased GC if we allocate policy objects per-request.

ash: Another angle: split responsibilities by invariants — queue topology = physical placement + affinity. Admission = policy decisions (deadline hints, tenant credits). That makes rollout safer: we can change policies without touching placement.

maria: Exactly. The plan I prototyped: scheduler loads a QueueTopology from a provider interface. AdmissionController implements: ShouldAdmit(RequestMeta) -> AdmitResult (admit/queue/evict). Scheduler calls it at enqueue time.

kevin: Can you paste the interface you used?

maria: Sure:

```go
// minimal interface
type AdmissionController interface {
  ShouldAdmit(req *RequestMeta) (AdmitResult, error)
}

// AdmitResult: { Admit bool, Reason string, LeaseMs int }
```

alex: LeaseMs is interesting. You mean a soft lease so scheduler can reserve headroom?

maria: Yes — if controller returns LeaseMs>0 scheduler reserves tokens for that duration avoiding head-of-line blocking from tiny requests. Also helps cooperative preemption.

ash: How are you representing queues? Is it lane-per-priority or dynamic binning?

maria: Lane-per-priority for now (simple arrays of lists) with optional tenant affinity buckets. The topology provider can emit N lanes and a mapping function: RequestMeta -> laneID.

kevin: We should avoid per-request locks at enqueue path. Use sharded queues with per-shard CAS pointers; admission controller can be read-only in the fast path (cached decision) to avoid heavy sync.

maria: Good point — implemented a tiny LRU cache for controller decisions keyed by request fingerprint. Misses go to controller RPC. Cache TTL is short (100ms) to avoid stale fairness distortions.

alex: For Dedicated/Private deployments, RPC to controller might cross process boundaries. We need a local fallback policy when controller isn't reachable. What do you have?

maria: Fallback = conservative admit (admit only latency-sensitive tiny requests up to N tokens) plus degrade to FIFO. We log metrics and surface a rollout flag in Console.

ash: Metrics to add: admit_rate_by_tenant, lease_usage, controller_rtt_p95, cache_hit_rate, enqueue_latency_p99. Those will help decide if RPC hop is acceptable.

kevin: For testing, we should add a microbench that simulates 10k rps with mixed sizes and toggles controller local vs remote to measure p99 token latency. Also chaos test where controller fails mid-load.

maria: Already added unit + integration tests, microbench next. One design question: do we expose a minimal runtime API to plugins (e.g., policy writers)? Something like:

```proto
service AdmissionPlugin {
  rpc Evaluate(EvalRequest) returns (EvalResponse);
}

message EvalRequest { RequestMeta meta = 1; }
message EvalResponse { bool admit = 1; int32 lease_ms = 2; string reason = 3; }
```

alex: Sounds fine. Keep plugin sandboxed. No direct memory access — just protobuf. That'll let SRE write a policy without rebuilding runtime.

kevin: One more: eviction strategy when queue is overloaded. If controller says evict, who picks which queued requests to drop? Scheduler should own that to keep data structures localized. Controller can return eviction hint (tenant, priority).

maria: Agreed — controller returns eviction_hint list, scheduler does best-effort scan in lanes to evict. We should include stable eviction scoring to reproduce behavior across restarts.

ash: Rollout: feature-flag the topology extraction first (in-proc), then flip admission to controller with cache, then add RPC-only controller in canary region, measure metrics, then enable globally.

maria: Proposed canary checklist: 1) controller_rtt_p95 < 2ms in canary 2) cache_hit_rate > 80% under load 3) no p99 increase > 10% for tail-sensitive routes 4) automated rollback if admission_error_rate > 0.5%

kevin: + add synthetic workload that stresses head-of-line to validate lease behavior.

ash: Sounds good. Small nit: document stable serialization for QueueTopology to ease hot reloads.

maria: Will add docs + migration script. Planning to cut the PR today and run microbench tomorrow. Anyone want to pair on chaos tests?

alex: I can join tomorrow morning PST.

kevin: Happy to help with microbench infra.

ash: I'll write the policy fallback and a sample plugin.

sre-bot: Deployment note: when canary flips controller RPC we will need to bump circuit-breaker timeout to 50ms for the first 24h.

maria: Nice — thanks all. If no objections, I'll merge the topology extract PR by EOD and create the canary playbook. :rocket:
